title: Inside Neo4j: native graph storage, memory and clustering
goal: By the end, you can explain how Neo4j stores a graph so that following a link costs the same at any size, decide how much of a server's memory it keeps for its files, say what its log does in a crash, back up the free edition, and say what a group of servers adds.
opening:
Picture a wall of lockers at a train station, all the same width and numbered from 0. Locker 2 holds a note from a friend: "open 28". Locker 28 says "open 26", and so on. You never need a map, because you can count your way to any locker.

Now picture a payments company's fraud team. Their map shows who is linked to whom: accounts, the phones they log in from, and the money they send each other. It finds the close links of a suspicious account in a millisecond. Next year the map will be a thousand times bigger. Will the same question take a thousand times longer?

Most people guess yes, because almost every lookup in this track grew with the data. Through the last twelve lessons, up to Materialized views and data cubes, we built a database's parts one at a time. In this lesson, we'll take a real one, Neo4j, apart: read its files byte by byte, find those parts, and crash it on purpose. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.

warmup.q: The fraud team's map has just been loaded into a graph database: 37 links between accounts, phones and devices. The database has told the loading program that every save is safe. It keeps links in a file of their own, 34 bytes per link. How big is that file on the disk at that moment?
options: 37 x 34 = 1,258 bytes: one slot for each link
8,192 bytes: one page, the fixed-size block the database reads and writes its files in
0 bytes: nothing has been written to it yet
More than 1,258 bytes, because the file also needs an index to find each link
warmup.why: It's 0 bytes, as the third section shows. A save counts as safe once it's in a different file, the transaction log, which the database only adds to at the end and forces onto the disk. The link file is filled in later, at a checkpoint: every 15 minutes, every 100,000 saves, or when the server stops cleanly. One page, 8,192 bytes, is what the file grew to after a clean stop, which makes it the tempting answer. And no index is needed to find a link, as the first section shows.

sections.h: Fixed-size records: how Neo4j follows a link by multiplying
sections.body:
Let's start with the fraud team's map, as the Data models track's lesson Graph databases with Neo4j and Cypher built it. A **graph** here is a set of things and the links between them. Each thing is a node: 13 accounts, 9 devices and 6 phone numbers. Each link is a relationship, and it has a type: `USES` when an account logs in from a device or phone, `TRANSFERRED_TO` when one account sends money to another. A node also has a label that says what kind of thing it is, such as `Account`, and properties, named values such as `id: 'A-3101'`.

Neo4j is a database program built to store graphs, and Cypher is the language you ask it questions in. A running Neo4j is called a server, because it serves the programs that connect to it, its clients.

The fraud team's question is a walk: start at A-3101, follow its relationships to its neighbours, then theirs. Each step along one relationship is a hop, and the price of a hop sets the price of the walk.

The obvious way to store a graph is a table of nodes, plus a link table with one row per relationship that holds the ids of its two ends. To find A-3101's relationships, the database searches the link table with an index, a lookup structure that finds rows by a value. Here it's a B+tree, the sorted tree of pages from the lesson B+trees. It reads one page per level, from the top down. At 100,000 rows the tree is 3 levels deep, and at 10 million it's 4. So a hop costs a search, and the search grows, slowly, with the whole graph.

Now remember the lockers. Make every record the same size and give it a number, its id. Record N then starts at byte N x size of its file, and finding it is arithmetic. Neo4j's record format does exactly that. A-3101 is node 2, and it lives at byte 2 x 15 = 30 of a file called `neostore.nodestore.db`. Relationship 28 lives at byte 28 x 34 = 952 of `neostore.relationshipstore.db`. Neo4j finds both without searching. It calls this index-free adjacency: finding a node's neighbours without an index.

A node record is 15 bytes. It holds a flag (a yes-or-no marker) that says it's in use, then the ids of the node's first relationship and first property record. Its labels and one more flag fill the rest. A relationship record is 34 bytes: its two nodes, its type, four pointers to other relationships, its first property record and two flags. A pointer here is the id of another record. A property record is 41 bytes, with room for four 8-byte values. Neo4j moves its files in pages of 8 KB (8,192 bytes), like the heap files of the lesson Pages, tuples and heap files. Its `aligned` format, the layout the lab's Neo4j uses, leaves the end of each page empty, so no record sits across two pages. A page holds 546 node records or 240 relationship records.

The four pointers make it a graph. A node's relationships form a chain: each one points to the next, the way each locker's note names the next locker. Each also points back to the one before, so the chain is a doubly linked list. A relationship belongs to two chains, one for each of its nodes, so it holds a previous and a next pointer for each. The lab calls them `firstPrev`, `firstNext`, `secondPrev` and `secondNext`. A new relationship goes in at the front of both chains, the head, so a chain reads newest first. The head has no previous record, so Neo4j stores the chain's length there. That's the node's degree, its number of relationships, and it costs two reads.

**Record N lives at byte N x size. Find the first node once, then multiply.**

The locker picture breaks at size. Walking to locker 30,000 takes longer than walking to locker 3, but 30,000 x 34 is no slower to work out than 3 x 34. What takes time is reading the record, and next we'll see why.

aside.title: If multiplying is so fast, why doesn't every database do it?
aside.body: Because it only works when every record has the same size, and most data doesn't. A row in a payments table holds a shop name that may be 3 characters or 300. So PostgreSQL uses slotted pages instead, where a small list at the top of each page says where each row starts (the lesson Pages, tuples and heap files). Neo4j pays for its fixed sizes elsewhere: a long string doesn't fit in a record, so it spills into more records and costs more reads. And an id says nothing about what's inside the record. To find the account called A-3101, Neo4j still searches a B+tree, once, at the start of the walk.

sections.h: Two kinds of memory: the page cache for the files, the heap for the queries
sections.body:
A hop is one multiplication and one read, and the read decides the speed. Reading from memory (RAM, the fast working memory that forgets everything when the power goes) takes about 100 nanoseconds (billionths of a second). Reading from an SSD, the disk that keeps data through a power cut, takes about 100 microseconds (millionths of a second): a thousand times longer. So a fraud walk that reads 2,000 records takes 0.2 ms (thousandths of a second) when every page is in memory. It can take 200 ms when every read goes to the disk. That's why Neo4j keeps its files in memory, in its own page cache.

The page cache is a buffer pool, the idea of the lesson The buffer pool. It's a fixed amount of memory, cut into 8 KB slots, that holds copies of pages from the files, and `server.memory.pagecache.size` sets how much. To read a record, Neo4j asks the cache for its page. If the page is there, that's a hit, and the read is a memory access. If not, that's a miss: Neo4j reads the page from its file, first throwing out a page nobody has used for a while if the cache is full. A page that a change has touched is dirty, and it stays in the cache until a checkpoint writes it back (the next section).

You may be thinking, "The operating system already keeps recently used files in memory." It does: the kernel, the core of the operating system, keeps a page cache, which the lesson The page cache, writeback and fsync explains. Neo4j keeps its own anyway, so it decides which pages stay and when dirty pages reach the disk. Its indexes live there too, because they're B+trees in pages.

Neo4j is written in Java, and a Java program keeps its working objects in a region of memory called the heap. Everything that isn't a page goes there: query plans (the steps Neo4j chose to answer a query), the rows a query is working on, and each transaction's changes. A transaction is a group of changes saved together or not at all, and commit is the moment they're saved. A `CREATE` of 2,000 relationships keeps all 2,000 in the heap until it commits. Java's garbage collector, which frees objects nobody uses, pauses the program now and then, and the pauses grow with the heap. Above about 31 GB, Java also stops storing the links between its objects in a short 4-byte form, so a bigger heap holds less per gigabyte.

So size the two for different things. The page cache should hold all the files and indexes, with room to grow: Neo4j's manual adds 20% to their size, so 35 GB becomes 42 GB. The heap should fit the queries and transactions that run at the same time, usually a few GB and at most 31 GB. Set its starting size equal to its largest (`server.memory.heap.initial_size` and `server.memory.heap.max_size`), so Java never stops to resize it. Leave the operating system at least a gigabyte, and more for full-text or vector indexes, which it caches itself.

The trap is that a small test graph fits in any cache, so a server left at the defaults looks fine until the real graph arrives. `neo4j-admin`, Neo4j's tool for looking after a server, suggests a split with `server memory-recommendation`, and the Try it runs it. Treat that as a start: it doesn't know how big your files will grow. Next, we'll see what happens to the dirty pages when the power goes.

sections.h: Every commit goes to the transaction log first, and the files catch up later
sections.body:
Right after the fraud graph is loaded, the relationship file, `neostore.relationshipstore.db`, is 0 bytes long. That was the warm-up's answer. All 37 relationships are in the page cache, and on the disk they're in a 15,715-byte file called `neostore.transaction.db.0`.

Here's why. One commit can change pages in four or five files: the node file, the relationship file, the property file, an index. Writing them all at commit would scatter writes across the disk on every transaction. Worse, a crash halfway through would leave half a relationship on disk, linked into one node's chain and not the other's.

So Neo4j does what the lesson Write-ahead logging and crash recovery describes. A log is a file you only ever add to at the end, like a notebook you never rub out. At commit, Neo4j adds the transaction's changes to the end of its transaction log: one write, in one place. Then it calls fsync, which makes the operating system write those bytes to the disk now instead of later. Only then does it apply the changes to the pages in the page cache. The commit is durable, safe through a crash, once the log is on disk, even though the other files are behind.

The files catch up at a checkpoint. Neo4j writes every dirty page back to its file and notes in `checkpoint.0` how far the files are now complete. By default that happens every 15 minutes or every 100,000 transactions (`db.checkpoint.interval.time` and `db.checkpoint.interval.tx`), and always on a clean shutdown. After a crash, the files are as old as the last checkpoint. So at startup Neo4j replays the log from there, applying each change again, in order. That's recovery, and the Try it crashes the server to watch it.

Other copies catch up by reading the log too: the backups of Enterprise Edition, the paid version of Neo4j, and the other servers of a cluster (the last section). Neo4j starts a new log file at 256 MiB, about 268 million bytes (`db.tx_log.rotation.size`), and keeps 2 days and 2 GB of old ones by default (`db.tx_log.rotation.retention_policy`). Put the `data/transactions` folder on a fast disk, because every commit waits for it.

And the indexes? They live in the `schema/index` folder, and they answer the one question a walk can't: where to start. Every database begins with two token lookup indexes: one lists the nodes of each label, and one the relationships of each type. A uniqueness constraint on `Account.id`, a rule that no two accounts share an id, adds a range index: a B+tree in its own folder under `schema/index/range-1.0`. In a Cypher plan, the start of the walk becomes `NodeUniqueIndexSeek`: one search for one node. After that, the walk never touches an index again.

Next, we'll look at what you touch when you run a server.

sections.h: Running one server: a settings file, a data folder and one tool
sections.body:
Everything so far ran on one server, and running one comes down to one file, one folder and one tool.

The file is `conf/neo4j.conf`. It holds plain `key=value` settings, and the ones you set on the first day are few:

```properties
# listen on every interface (the default is localhost only)
server.default_listen_address=0.0.0.0
# the address clients and routing tables are given
server.default_advertised_address=graph-1.internal
# Bolt, for drivers and cypher-shell; HTTP, for the API and the browser
server.bolt.listen_address=:7687
server.http.listen_address=:7474
server.memory.heap.initial_size=8g
server.memory.heap.max_size=8g
server.memory.pagecache.size=24g
server.directories.transaction.logs.root=/fastdisk/transactions
db.tx_log.rotation.retention_policy=2 days 2G
dbms.security.auth_enabled=true
```

The first four settings say where clients can reach the server. `0.0.0.0` means on every network the machine is on, and the advertised address is the name the server gives out for itself. A port, such as `:7687`, is a number that says which program on a machine a connection is for (the Computer networking track explains ports). Bolt is Neo4j's own protocol, the rules programs and `cypher-shell` use to talk to it, and HTTP, the web's protocol, serves Neo4j's web tools. Then come the memory sizes, the log's folder and how long to keep it, and the switch that turns on passwords.

In Docker you don't edit the file. An environment variable is a named value handed to a program when it starts. Each one that begins with `NEO4J_` becomes a setting, with `_` in place of each dot and `__` in place of each `_`. So `NEO4J_server_memory_pagecache_size` is `server.memory.pagecache.size`.

The folder is `data/`. `data/databases/<name>/` holds one database's files and its `schema/index/` folder, `data/transactions/<name>/` its transaction log, and `data/dumps/` the backups `neo4j-admin` writes. Next to it, `logs/` has `neo4j.log`, `debug.log` (where the recovery line was), `query.log` and `security.log`. A server always has two databases: `system`, which holds users, their permissions and the list of databases, and `neo4j`, the default one for your data.

The tool is `neo4j-admin`, and its jobs follow from the files. `neo4j-admin database import full` builds the files straight from CSV files (plain text, one record per line, values split by commas) while the database is stopped (offline). Skipping transactions and the log makes it the fastest first load for hundreds of millions of records. `dump` writes one database to a single compressed file, and `load` puts one back; both need the database offline. `info` reads a database's format and whether it needs recovery, `check` makes sure its records agree with each other, and `migrate` moves it to another format.

Community Edition, the free version this lab runs, stops there. It runs one server with one database for your data, so `CREATE DATABASE` fails. It has no online backup, a copy taken while the server keeps working, so you stop the server and run `dump`. It has no clusters. Enterprise Edition adds online `neo4j-admin database backup` and `restore`, full or of only what changed since the last one, and the cluster of the next section.

A server you stop for every backup may be fine for a copy you can rebuild. Next, we'll see what a group of servers adds when it isn't.

sections.h: A group of servers: primaries that vote and secondaries that read
sections.body:
One server is one thing that can fail. If it crashes, the fraud graph is out of reach until the server restarts and replays its log. If its disk dies, you're back to the last dump. Neo4j's answer is a cluster, a group of servers that keep copies of the same database, and it's in Enterprise only.

Picture a committee that keeps the official minutes. A decision counts once most members have written it into their own copy, so the minutes survive any one member falling ill. In a cluster, each copy of a database is a primary or a secondary, and the primaries are the committee. They follow Raft, a set of rules for agreeing on one log, which the Consistency and consensus track builds step by step. Here you need only its main rule: a write counts as committed once a majority of the primaries have it in their logs.

The primaries choose one of them as the writer, like the committee's chair, and Raft calls it the leader, and every write transaction goes to it. The writer adds the transaction to its log, sends it to the other primaries, and commits once a majority have it: 2 of 3. The others apply it from there.

To survive F broken primaries, you need 2F + 1 of them: three survive one failure, and five survive two. The manual allows at most 11 primaries per database, and each extra one makes every write wait for one more server. If a majority is lost, the database stops taking writes. That's the price of never losing a committed one.

A secondary never votes. It pulls the transaction log from the primaries in its own time, applies it and answers reads. Secondaries add room for reads, up to 20 per database, and losing one only costs speed. Because they pull, they can be a little behind.

The committee picture breaks here: a member can see who chairs the meeting, but a program can't see which server is the writer. Its driver, the library a program uses to talk to a database, finds out. With a `neo4j://` address, the driver connects to any server and fetches a routing table, the list of servers that can write, read and route. It keeps the table for its TTL (time to live), 300 seconds, then fetches a fresh one. It sends each write transaction to the writer and spreads reads over the readers. A `bolt://` address means one particular server and no routing: point it at a primary that isn't the writer, and writes fail.

A program that writes and then reads at once may land on a secondary that hasn't caught up. So the driver passes a bookmark, a note naming the transaction it just committed, and the cluster runs the read only on a server that has applied it. That's read-your-writes, the first topic of the Replication track's lesson When followers lag.

The compare block shows the two settings a cluster adds to each server's `neo4j.conf`: where the servers find each other, and how many primaries a new database gets.

For the fraud graph, it's a question of downtime. A copy rebuilt from the payments records can live on one Community server. If card payments wait on risk flags read from the graph, run three primaries.

worked.title: Size the fraud graph's server from its record counts

steps.say: Start from the counts the fraud team expects in a year: 120 million nodes (50 million accounts, 70 million devices and phones), 1 billion relationships (400 million `USES`, 600 million `TRANSFERRED_TO`), and about one property record per node and per relationship.
steps.code:

relationships 1,000,000,000   34 bytes each   240 per page
property recs 1,120,000,000   41 bytes each   199 per page

steps.say: Turn counts into whole pages with the lab's `alignedStoreBytes`: the records, divided by the records per page, rounded up, times 8,192. A GiB is 2^30 bytes, a little more than a billion. Strings too long for a property record go to a separate file, so leave room for them in the estimate.

val nodes = alignedStoreBytes(120_000_000, NODE_RECORD_SIZE)      // 1.7 GiB

println((nodes + rels + props).toDouble() / gib)                 // 76.4

lab.title: Build Neo4j's record store: fixed-size records, relationship chains and a walk
steps: Run the tests from the `labs` folder. No Docker needed. One test passes, because it tests `locate`, which is given; seven fail.
Write `alignedStoreBytes`: whole pages, at least one. The test checks it against the file sizes Neo4j wrote in the Try-its: 8,192 bytes for 28 nodes and 73,728 for 2,037 relationships.

Write `createRelationship`, following the KDoc, the comment above the function. Link the new record in at the head of both chains, store the degree in the head's prev field, and fix up the old head. A test then rebuilds the fraud graph in the order Neo4j created it and compares your records with the bytes `od` showed in the first Try it.

Write `relationshipsOf` (walk one chain), `degree` (two reads) and `expand`, a breadth-first walk: every node one hop away, then every node two hops away, and so on. The last test adds 100,000 unrelated transfers. It checks that your walk reads exactly as many records as before, while the link-table model's B+tree searches get three times as deep. All eight pass.
hints: `alignedStoreBytes`: `val perPage = PAGE_SIZE / recordSize`, then `max(1L, (records + perPage - 1) / perPage) * PAGE_SIZE`.

In `createRelationship`, write a local `fun linkIn(node: Long): Pair<Long, Long>` that returns (degree, next) for the new record, and call it for `from`, then `to`. Use `old.copy(firstPrev = id, firstInFirstChain = false)` (or the second pair) to rewrite the old head.

Read the old head inside `linkIn`, after the call for `from` has finished. If the last relationship you created joined the same two nodes, both calls touch the same record, and the second must see the first one's write.
In a chain, the node is either `rel.firstNode` or `rel.secondNode`: pick `firstNext` or `secondNext` (and `firstPrev` or `secondPrev`) to match.
`expand`: keep a `seen` set with the start in it and a list of the nodes reached at each hop. Add a node to the result only the first time `seen.add(other)` returns true.

drill.title: A relationship record from memory
drill.prompt: Without looking: (a) list the fields of Neo4j's 34-byte relationship record; (b) A-3101 (node 2) has relationships 28, 26, 5 and 4, newest first. Write the pointers relationship 26 holds for A-3101, and say what relationship 28's prev field for A-3101 holds, and why; (c) say where a commit goes first, what a checkpoint does to the files, and what happens after a crash.

answer.src:
(a) in-use byte | first node | second node | type |
    first node's prev | first node's next | second node's prev | second node's next |
    first property | flags: head of the first chain, head of the second chain
    (1 + 8 x 4 + 1 = 34 bytes)
(b) relationship 26 is A-3101 -> A-3103, so A-3101 uses the FIRST pair:
    firstPrev = 28, firstNext = 5
    relationship 28 heads A-3101's chain, so it has no prev: that field holds
    the chain's length, A-3101's degree, 4
(c) the transaction log first (appended, fsync'ed at commit), then the pages in
    the page cache. A checkpoint writes the dirty pages to the store files; after
    a crash, recovery replays the log from the last checkpoint.

recap: Neo4j's record format keeps fixed-size records in files of 8 KB pages: nodes 15 bytes, relationships 34, properties 41. Record N starts at byte N x size, so a hop is a multiplication and a read, whatever the size of the graph.

A node's relationships form a chain, a doubly linked list through the relationship records, newest first. Each relationship sits in two chains, and the head of a chain stores the node's degree, so counting costs two reads.

The page cache, Neo4j's own buffer pool, should hold the files and indexes plus 20%. The Java heap holds plans, query rows and changes not yet committed; set its starting size equal to its largest, at most 31 GB.

A commit is added to the transaction log and forced to disk with fsync, then applied in the page cache. Checkpoints write the files (every 15 minutes or 100,000 transactions, and on shutdown), and recovery replays the log after a crash. Indexes only find where a walk starts.

Community is one server with one database for your data, backed up by stopping it and running `neo4j-admin database dump`. Enterprise adds online backups and clusters: primaries agree through Raft (2F + 1 of them survive F failures), secondaries pull the log to answer reads, and `neo4j://` drivers follow a routing table.

The limit: the record trick works only for things of one size. A long string spills into extra records, every write in a cluster waits for a majority, and a walk that fans out still pays for every path it explores.
closing:
We started with lockers whose notes name the next locker, and a fraud team asking whether a map a thousand times bigger means a thousand times the wait. For Neo4j it doesn't: a hop is a multiplication and a read, at any size. What changes the wait is whether the page is in memory.

Ask the next database you meet the three questions we asked of Neo4j. Where do its records live on the disk? Which memory holds them? Which file does a commit wait for? Its manual's page on file locations is a good start.

Next, we'll ask them of PostgreSQL, the database we've used all track, and find out why every connection to it costs a whole program.

quiz.q: The fraud graph grows from 1 million to 1 billion relationships. A query walks A-3101's four relationships, starting from its node record. How many record reads does that part of the walk take now?
options: About 3 times as many, like a B+tree that gained levels
The same five: one for the node, one per relationship
Twice as many, because each relationship is in two chains
It depends on whether the relationship type has an index
quiz.why: Record N is at byte N x 34, so reading the next relationship in a chain is arithmetic on its id, and the chain has as many records as the node has relationships. The size of the rest of the graph never comes into it. A B+tree search does get deeper as its table grows, which makes the first option tempting. Being in two chains doesn't double anything: the walk follows one of the two pairs of pointers. And a relationship is never found through an index.

quiz.q: Neo4j's machine runs out of memory, and the operating system kills Neo4j 10 minutes after its last checkpoint. Thousands of transactions were committed in those 10 minutes. What happens when it starts again?
options: Those transactions are lost, because the files only hold what the last checkpoint wrote
Neo4j replays the transaction log from the last checkpoint, and every committed transaction is back
Neo4j refuses to start until you run `neo4j-admin database check`
Only the transactions whose pages were still in the page cache are lost
quiz.why: A commit returns only after its changes are added to the transaction log and forced to the disk. The other files are behind by up to one checkpoint, and recovery replays the log from the last checkpoint to close the gap, as the Try it showed with "1 transactions applied". The page cache is lost in a crash, but nothing committed lived only there, which is why the first and last options fail. `check` makes sure the records agree with each other; recovery doesn't need it.

quiz.q: A server has 64 GB of memory. Neo4j's files and indexes take 40 GB, and they grow about 10% a year. Which settings are a sound start?
options: Heap 48 GB, page cache 8 GB, because queries need memory
Heap 31 GB, page cache 31 GB
Heap 12 GB, page cache 48 GB, and the rest for the operating system
No settings: the operating system's cache will hold the files
quiz.why: The page cache should hold all the files plus room to grow, 40 x 1.2 = 48 GB, or walks start reading from the disk. The heap needs to fit the queries and transactions that run at the same time, and 12 GB is plenty for most. A 48 GB heap also loses Java's short pointers and pauses longer. Neo4j keeps its files in its own page cache, so leaving it unset only gets a default that knows nothing about your files.

quiz.q: In Pages, tuples and heap files, PostgreSQL found a row by its page and slot: a small list at the top of the page says where in the page each row starts. Neo4j finds relationship 28 at byte 28 x 34. What does the slotted page give PostgreSQL that Neo4j's fixed-size records don't?
options: Rows of any length: the list lets a row of any size sit anywhere in the page, and move when the page is tidied, while its page and slot stay the same
Faster lookups, because reading the list is quicker than multiplying
Safety through crashes, because the list makes the write-ahead log unnecessary
Nothing, because both layouts can only store rows of one size
quiz.why: Fixed-size records make the address arithmetic, which is why a Neo4j hop costs a multiplication. The price is that anything longer than a record, such as a long string, must spill into other records and cost extra reads. A slotted page adds one step in between, so rows can vary in size and move inside the page without changing their address. Both layouts still need a log to survive a crash, and neither lookup is slow.

quiz.q: A program connects to a cluster of three primaries with `bolt://graph-2:7687`. graph-2 is a primary, but not the writer. What happens to the program's write transactions, and what's the fix?
options: graph-2 passes them on to the writer, so nothing needs fixing
They fail, because a `bolt://` connection doesn't route; use a `neo4j://` address so the driver fetches a routing table
They are written to graph-2 and copied to the others later
They wait until graph-2 becomes the writer
quiz.why: `bolt://` means one particular server, and a primary that isn't the writer doesn't accept writes. With `neo4j://`, the driver fetches a routing table (which servers can write, read and route, kept for its TTL) and sends each write transaction to the current writer, even after a new one is chosen. Writing to graph-2 and copying later would break Raft's promise that every commit is on a majority.

flashcards.front: How big are Neo4j's node, relationship and property records in its record format?
flashcards.back: 15, 34 and 41 bytes. Record N starts at byte N x size, so no index is needed to find it.

flashcards.front: What does a relationship record point to?
flashcards.back: Its two nodes, its type, the previous and next relationship in the first node's chain, the same two for the second node's chain, and its first property record.

flashcards.front: How can Neo4j count a node's relationships in two reads?
flashcards.back: The head of a chain has no previous record, so that field holds the chain's length: the node's degree.

flashcards.front: What goes in Neo4j's page cache, and what goes in its heap?
flashcards.back: Page cache: pages of the files and Neo4j's own indexes; size it to files plus indexes plus 20%. Heap: plans, query rows and changes not yet committed; starting size equal to largest, at most 31 GB.

flashcards.front: Where does a commit go first, and what does a checkpoint do?
flashcards.back: To the end of the transaction log, forced to disk with fsync, then into the page cache. A checkpoint writes the dirty pages to the files, and after a crash recovery replays the log from there.

flashcards.front: How do you back up Neo4j Community Edition?
flashcards.back: Stop the server and run `neo4j-admin database dump`; put it back with `load`. Online backup is Enterprise only.
`neo4j://` fetches a routing table and sends writes to the cluster's writer and reads to readers. `bolt://` talks to one server only.

terms.plain: Finding a node's neighbours by following ids stored in its records, with no index search.
A node's relationships as a doubly linked list through the relationship records, newest first.
A node's number of relationships, which Neo4j keeps in the head record of the node's chain.
Neo4j's own buffer pool: memory cut into 8 KB slots that hold pages of its files and indexes.
The memory where a Java program keeps its objects; in Neo4j, plans, query rows and changes not yet committed.
Writing the page cache's dirty pages to the files and noting how far they're complete, so recovery starts there.
Copies of a database in a cluster. Primaries vote and commit each write on a majority; secondaries pull the log and answer reads.
The list of servers that can write, read and route, which a `neo4j://` driver fetches and keeps for its TTL.

explain_back.prompt: A friend who has looked after other databases is about to run Neo4j for the fraud team. Explain how Neo4j stores the graph, what the page cache and the heap are for and how to size them, what happens in a crash, and what the free Community Edition gives you next to a cluster.
explain_back.answer: Neo4j keeps fixed-size records in files: nodes are 15 bytes, relationships 34 and properties 41. Record N starts at byte N times the record size, so following a relationship is arithmetic on an id, not an index search, and it costs the same however big the graph gets. Each node's relationships are a doubly linked list threaded through the relationship records, newest first, and each relationship sits in two of those lists. Indexes are used only to find where a walk starts. Neo4j reads its files through its own page cache, a buffer pool of 8 KB pages. I'd size it to the files plus indexes plus 20%, because a walk that misses goes to the disk, about a thousand times slower. The heap holds plans, query rows and changes not yet committed: set its starting size equal to its largest, and stay at or under 31 GB. A commit is added to the transaction log and forced to disk with fsync, the files catch up at checkpoints every 15 minutes or 100,000 transactions, and after a crash Neo4j replays the log from the last checkpoint, so nothing committed is lost. Community is one server with one database for your data, and a backup means stopping it and running neo4j-admin database dump. Enterprise adds online backups and clusters: three primaries agree through Raft and survive one failure, secondaries pull the log to answer reads, and drivers with neo4j:// addresses send writes to the current writer.

deeper.body:
A node with thousands of relationships, such as a kiosk that thousands of customers have tapped, would make "only its outgoing transfers" read every one of them. So once a node passes 50 relationships (`db.relationship_grouping_threshold`), Neo4j splits its chain into relationship groups, one chain per type and direction, and the node record points at the groups instead. That's a dense node.

Property records are where most of the files go, and they hide a second level. Each 41-byte record has four 8-byte blocks. A small number or a short string fits in one or two blocks, inside the record. A longer string or a list spills into `neostore.propertystore.db.strings` or `.arrays`, as a chain of further records, so a long shop name costs extra reads. Property names aren't stored as text either: `amountMinor` is kept as a small number, a token, and the names live in `neostore.propertystore.db.index.keys`.

Ids are reused. When you delete a node, its id goes on a free list (the `.id` files next to each store file), and a later `CREATE` can get the same id. Any code that saved `id(n)` outside the database can then point at a different node. That's why the first Try it used `id()` only to find the bytes, and why Cypher 5 and Cypher 25 prefer `elementId()`, which is only promised to stay the same within one transaction anyway. Give each node a key of your own, such as `Account.id`, with a uniqueness constraint.

The `block` format was built to cut the pointer chasing this lesson walked through. Since version 5.22 it's the default for new databases in Enterprise Edition; Community stays on `aligned`, which `neo4j-admin database info` reports as `record-aligned-1.1`. In the record format, reading one node with its labels, properties and relationships can touch three or four files. In `block`, a node's small block (128 bytes, split into two 64-byte records) holds its labels, properties under about 31 bytes, and relationships, so one page read usually gets all of it. Bigger nodes spill into larger blocks of up to 8 KB, and dense nodes keep their relationships in a B+tree sorted by type and direction. Moving an Enterprise database is `neo4j-admin database migrate --to-format=block`, done offline, and it changes the internal ids. The `standard` and `high_limit` formats are deprecated, which means they still work but are on their way out, and the manual plans to end their support in November 2029.

Watching the page cache is an Enterprise feature in practice. Enterprise's metrics, the numbers a server reports about itself, include `page_cache.hits`, `page_cache.page_faults` and `page_cache.hit_ratio`. On Community 2026.10, `PROFILE` prints a "Page Cache Hits/Misses" column that the default slotted runtime (the engine that runs Cypher plans) leaves at 0/0, and `dbms.queryJmx` returns only Java's own counters. So the signs of a page cache that's too small are indirect: walks that slow down as the files grow, and disk reads on the store files while queries run.

Clusters also decide where each database lives. A server can hold some databases as a primary and others as a secondary, and `CREATE DATABASE ... TOPOLOGY 3 PRIMARIES 2 SECONDARIES` sets the copies for each database. The `system` database, which holds users and the list of databases, has its own Raft group, across the servers chosen with `server.cluster.system_database_mode`. Each database chooses its own writer, so writes to different databases can go to different servers.
